title: setMigrator has no in-flight-position guard, allowing a successor migrator to claim NFTs deposited by a predecessor migrator
drop_reason: Centralization framing without new privilege. The owner already controls migrator assignment; rotating the role gives the new migrator exactly the same powers as the old migrator. No plan deviation is identified (the plan does not specify any setMigrator timing invariant) and no state-machine bug holds even with the owner/role acting in good faith — by design, the new migrator inherits the role's powers. The underlying concern that the migrator can drain in-flight stakeFor-deposited NFTs is already captured by DEDUP-01 (which addresses the unstakeFor surface itself). The rotation-timing flavor is a hardening recommendation that falls below the sanitization bar per the parent CLAUDE.md known-invalid list ('reckless admin mistakes' / 'the owner could do X' without a concrete loss-of-funds path beyond documented role power).
description:
`setMigrator` (lines 244-247) updates the `migrator` storage slot without checking whether any positions deposited via the predecessor migrator are still outstanding, and without snapshotting which migrator a position was opened under. Combined with `unstakeFor` (line 543) routing NFTs to `msg.sender == migrator`, a rotation of the migrator role mid-flight has the effect that the NEW migrator can call `unstakeFor` on positions that the OLD migrator opened and collect the NFT principal, even though the OLD migrator was the entity that sourced the NFTs.

This is structurally related to DEDUP-01 but concerns specifically the migrator-rotation timing rather than the migrator-vs-direct-staker mixing. It is preserved as a separate finding because (a) the attack scenario is distinct (rotation event triggers re-attribution of in-flight principal), and (b) the mitigation is distinct (gate `setMigrator` on `totalStaked == 0`, or snapshot depositor per position) and applies even if `unstakeFor` is retained.

Other state-changing setters that affect accounting (`setDispatcherIndex`, `setNFTMinter`, `setStakedId`, `setTargetAPY`) all either gate on `totalStaked == 0` or settle accrual via `_updatePool` before mutating. `setMigrator` does neither. While the migrator role doesn't directly touch the accrual maths (so an `_updatePool` call is not needed for solvency reasons), the asymmetry between 'migrator who deposited' and 'migrator who can withdraw' is a structural inconsistency: once the migrator changes, the principal economics of in-flight positions silently re-attribute to the new migrator address.

Code references:
- `lib/phoenix-nft-staking/src/NFTStakerV2.sol:244-247` — `setMigrator`, no state guards.
- `lib/phoenix-nft-staking/src/NFTStakerV2.sol:543-562` — `unstakeFor`, NFTs to current `msg.sender`.
- `lib/phoenix-nft-staking/src/NFTStakerV2.sol:521-541` — `stakeFor`, no association between depositor and position recorded.
impact: Operational risk for the owner: rotating the migrator mid-migration (e.g. helper bug-fix mid-cycle) transfers the *future* `unstakeFor` proceeds for all existing `stakeFor`-deposited positions to the new migrator. If the predecessor migrator was a stateless helper that pulled NFTs from `NFTMinterV2` via `mintFor` (as in the documented `MigrationHelper.migrateAndStake`), the predecessor never recorded ownership — but the trust assumption is still that the entity that sourced the NFTs is the entity that can withdraw them, and rotation breaks that assumption silently. There is no event or revert path to surface this — the rotation just changes who gets the NFTs on the next `unstakeFor` call.
recommendation: Pick one of: (a) require `totalStaked == 0` in `setMigrator` (most restrictive, blocks mid-cycle rotation but matches the pattern of other setters); (b) record per-position depositor in the `UserInfo` struct so `unstakeFor` can verify the caller against the original depositor; or (c) remove the entire `unstakeFor` surface (matching the migration plan, see DEDUP-01). Option (c) is the smallest code change and matches the documented design; option (a) preserves `unstakeFor` while removing the rotation pitfall.
attack_scenario:
1. Owner sets migrator = `HelperA`. `HelperA` pulls NFTs from `NFTMinterV2` via `migrateMint(amount, address(this))` and calls `staker.stakeFor(user, amount)`. `HelperA` never held the NFTs across calls (the helper immediately forwards them to the staker via `safeTransferFrom` inside `stakeFor`).
2. Owner discovers a bug in `HelperA` and calls `setMigrator(HelperB)`.
3. `HelperB` (or its operator, if `HelperB` has an admin path) calls `unstakeFor(user, users[user].amount)`. The NFTs land in `HelperB`'s wallet. `HelperA`, despite being the entity that originally sourced them via the burn-and-mint flow, has no claim.
4. The user receives their pending phUSD via `_safePay(user, pending)` but their NFT principal is now in `HelperB`'s wallet rather than `HelperA`'s. Whether `HelperB` re-stakes or absconds is at `HelperB`'s discretion.
